digest.top_line: RTOG 1112: SBRT + sorafenib mOS 15.8 vs 12.3 mo, HR 0.77 (90% CI 0.59-1.01), not significant; mPFS HR 0.55 in locally advanced HCC.
digest.tldr: RT was the question at both sites. RTOG 1112 adds SBRT to sorafenib in locally advanced HCC: OS missed its unadjusted test (HR 0.77, 1-sided P=.06), mPFS HR 0.55; accrual stopped early after systemic SOC changed. ReCOG HNSCC reirradiation consensus hit ≥85% agreement on 24/31 statements (no ENI, definitive IMRT ~66 Gy), none backed by randomised data.

sites.intro: ReCOG ties curative reRT to Ward RPA class and to cumulative OAR EQD2 limits (carotid 120-125 Gy, mandible 114-119 Gy). Agreement was weakest on the cord and brainstem limits.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International expert consensus: a ReCOG core group drafted statements, then a **17-member radiation oncology panel** voted once on **31 statements**. Thresholds were high ≥85%, moderate 70-84%, low <70%, with no-opinion votes counted in the denominator. **24 (77%)** reached high consensus.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Recurrent or second primary **HNSCC in a previously irradiated field**, covering definitive and postoperative reirradiation. **Nasopharyngeal cancer and rare histologies excluded.** Evidence levels adapted from Oxford CEBM, level 1 (randomised) to level 4 (expert consensus).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Definitive:** CTV = GTV + 5 mm, no ENI, IMRT ~66 Gy for >25 cc, IMRT or SBRT for ≤25 cc, SBRT ~40 Gy in five fractions. **Postoperative:** primary-RT CTV rules, IMRT preferred, ~60 Gy. Cumulative doses in **EQD2 with α/β 2-3 Gy**, voxel-wise summation with DIR when available, with conservative manual point-dose addition acceptable otherwise.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **Carotid:** avoid cumulative EQD2 >120-125 Gy (α/β=2); encasement >180° and prior ulceration add risk. **Mandible:** ORN risk rises above 114-119 Gy EQD2. **Cord/brainstem:** D0.1 cc ≤50 and ≤55 Gy as targets, ~60 Gy at the surface case by case, recovery factors (10-25%) only with caution.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Split-course chemo-reRT in RTOG 9610 and RTOG 9911 gave 2-year OS of 15.2% and 25.9%, with grade 3-4 toxicity up to 34% and treatment-related mortality around 8%. The IMRT-era Ward cohort (n=412) reported median OS 16.5 mo with fatal toxicity in 1%. **GORTEC-GETTEC** (n=130), the randomised postop trial, improved locoregional control and RFS with **no OS benefit**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents recurrent or second primary non-nasopharyngeal HNSCC in an irradiated field treated with definitive or postoperative reirradiation. Does not represent nasopharyngeal cancer, rare histologies, or recurrence within 6 months outside urgent palliation.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Guidance for RPA class II and III rests largely on one retrospective RPA model, since most reirradiation outcome data come from RPA class I pts. The IMRT vs SBRT split and the dose statements come from non-randomised multi-institutional cohorts. The 10-25% recovery factor has very low evidence.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The seven moderate-consensus statements cluster on poor-prognosis subgroups, dose and fractionation, and SBRT, and the **lowest agreement (70%)** falls on cord and brainstem cumulative limits. The authors present dose thresholds and OAR constraints as pragmatic targets rather than validated limits. Sequencing reirradiation against first-line ICI has **no randomised data**.

studies.interpretation:
This statement mostly codifies practice that changed with IMRT; it does not propose new practice. The split-course chemoradiation of RTOG 9610 and RTOG 9911 carried treatment-related mortality around 8%, and the conformal-era retrospective series that followed reported lower severe and fatal toxicity. The panel's algorithm is built on those later series. Its practical contribution is a sequence a department can adopt and cite. Selection is gated on interval since prior RT, resection status, and organ dysfunction using the Ward RPA classes, technique follows target volume and subsite, and the plan is built against cumulative EQD2 limits. A reader already treating with IMRT to 60-66 Gy without elective nodes will find that most statements confirm current practice.

The main caution is that agreement and evidence are separate axes. The paper reports both, and they should be read separately. Elective nodal omission reached 100% agreement at evidence level 3, and it rests largely on one multi-institutional retrospective cohort of 505 pts. That cohort also supplies the 66 Gy dose statement. A dose gradient in a retrospective reirradiation series is open to confounding by indication: pts with smaller targets, better performance status, and more distance from critical organs are the ones who can be taken to full dose. The 2-year OS spread of 49.3% vs 34.2% vs 30.4% across dose bands likely mixes a dose effect with selection. That fits the moderate 82% agreement and the authors' preference for a dose corridor over a single number.

The IMRT vs SBRT split follows the same logic. In the Vargo multi-institutional comparison, the RPA class II OS gap favoring IMRT (35.4% vs 18.6%) disappeared once SBRT was restricted to 35 Gy or more on small targets. That fits SBRT losing efficacy as volume rises. It fits equally well with the unrestricted SBRT group carrying lower doses and less favorable pts. The 25 cc cut is therefore a defensible working boundary, not a demonstrated threshold. It does not show SBRT fails on a target just above it, only that no one has shown it works there. The caution for larynx and hypopharynx is the firmer constraint, because that toxicity signal is large and specific to subsite, not a between-technique comparison.

The organ-at-risk panel is where the document is weakest, and it says so. Cord and brainstem cumulative limits drew the lowest agreement (70%), recovery factors carry very low evidence, and the carotid thresholds come from retrospective series. Because no-opinion votes counted against agreement, a moderate label may reflect abstention as much as dissent. These numbers work best as planning targets to document deviations against, not as tolerance data.

What the statement leaves open is as useful as what it settles. It does not answer how to sequence reirradiation with first-line checkpoint inhibition, how protons compare with IMRT, or whether hyperfractionation helps outside nasopharynx, and it excludes nasopharyngeal disease entirely. The evidence most likely to move its moderate-consensus statements would be a prospective comparison of SBRT and IMRT stratified by volume, or prospective cumulative-dose toxicity data for serial organs.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Subsite, not only volume, gates SBRT: in Vargo's 291-pt series severe toxicity reached up to 50% for laryngeal or hypopharyngeal recurrences vs 6-20% at other subsites. Postop SBRT data are thin (n=28), so IMRT is preferred after salvage surgery.

studies.significance: PFS carries the RT signal: HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.40-0.75) with personalized 27.5-50 Gy in 5 fractions, in a cohort with 74.0% macrovascular invasion and no rise in G3+ TRAE (47% vs 42%). In-liver control and failure patterns are not reported in source text, so the case for liver SBRT rests on PFS plus an adjusted OS HR.
studies.monday_clinic: In locally advanced HCC with macrovascular invasion, unsuitable for or refractory to local-regional therapy, this supports weighing liver SBRT with first-line systemic therapy for progression control; it does not extend to pts on the newer systemic standard that ended accrual.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3 randomized**, multicenter, 1:1, stratified by performance status, liver function, degree of metastases and macrovascular invasion. **193 randomized, 177 eligible**; data collected April 2013 to March 2021. **Accrual stopped early** after a change in standard-of-care systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: HCC **unsuitable for or refractory to standard local-regional therapies**, candidates for first-line systemic therapy. Median age 66 (IQR 60-72), 84.7% male, **macrovascular invasion 74.0%**.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Sorafenib** in both arms; the experimental arm received SBRT followed by sorafenib.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Personalized SBRT, 27.5 to 50 Gy in 5 fractions.** Dose-selection rules, target volumes and OAR constraints not reported in source text.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** overall survival. **Secondary:** PFS, adverse events, quality of life.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary OS **not statistically significant** on the unadjusted test; significant after stratification-factor adjustment. **PFS clearly improved** with SBRT; values in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ treatment-related AEs **not increased** with SBRT. Treatment-related deaths: 2 with sorafenib (death NOS, liver failure), 1 with SBRT plus sorafenib (lung infection).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Radioembolization trials against or combined with sorafenib (SARAH, SIRveNIB, SORAMIC) did not show an OS gain. START, which tested TACE plus RT against sorafenib in macrovascular invasion, favored the radiation-containing arm, and RTOG 1112 points the same direction with stereotactic delivery.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents locally advanced HCC unsuitable for or refractory to local-regional therapy, 74.0% with macrovascular invasion, starting first-line sorafenib. Does not represent pts eligible for standard local-regional therapy or on newer first-line systemic regimens.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Analysis restricted to **177 eligible** of 193 randomized. **Local control and in-liver failure patterns not reported in source text**, and personalized 27.5-50 Gy dosing confounds any dose-response read. QoL rests on **17 and 20 evaluable pts**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors call the OS gain **clinically important but not statistically significant**; adjusted OS and PFS point the same way, so underpowering after early closure is a more plausible reason for the miss than absence of effect. It does not settle whether SBRT adds to the systemic standard that replaced sorafenib.

studies.interpretation:
RTOG 1112 asked whether liver SBRT extends survival when added to first-line sorafenib in locally advanced HCC that local-regional therapy could not address, a population in which intrahepatic progression is the usual way the disease declares itself. On its own primary test the answer is no: OS HR 0.77 with a 90% CI of 0.59-1.01 and a one-sided P=.06. Every other efficacy read points the same way, though. Median OS moved from 12.3 to 15.8 mo, the stratification-adjusted OS HR was 0.72 (95% CI 0.52-0.99), and the PFS HR of 0.55 had an upper bound of 0.75. A trial that misses its primary endpoint while its secondary estimates cohere is more plausibly underpowered than null, and here there is a concrete reason for underpowering: accrual closed early when the systemic standard changed.

That reading still has limits a skeptic would press. The adjusted OS analysis is a secondary lens, and a reader should not promote it to the primary result because it crossed 0.05. The analysis covers 177 eligible pts out of 193 randomized, a departure from intention-to-treat whose direction of bias the source does not let us judge. The source also does not state how progression was assessed or whether imaging review was blinded, and post-SBRT liver changes can complicate response calls, which matters because PFS carries the strongest signal.

For a radiation oncologist the population is the point. Macrovascular invasion was present in 74.0%, the phenotype in which tumor thrombus threatens liver function and where systemic therapy alone has historically struggled to hold intrahepatic disease. The PFS gain is consistent with SBRT controlling the dominant liver burden, but local control and patterns of failure are not reported in source text, so that mechanism is inferred rather than shown. Dosing was personalized across 27.5 to 50 Gy in 5 fractions, which speaks to feasibility across a range of liver function but prevents any dose-response read. Toxicity did not obviously rise: grade 3+ treatment-related AEs were 47% vs 42% (P=.52), with 1 treatment-related death after SBRT plus sorafenib against 2 with sorafenib alone. The quality-of-life difference, 35% vs 10% improved at 6 mo, sits on 17 and 20 evaluable pts and should be read as hypothesis only.

Against prior liver-directed radiation data, the result lines up with START, which tested TACE plus RT against sorafenib in macrovascular invasion and favored the radiation-containing arm, and departs from the radioembolization trials SARAH, SIRveNIB and SORAMIC, none of which showed an OS gain against or alongside sorafenib. RTOG 1112 is a multicenter phase 3 test of stereotactic external-beam delivery in this setting, so its direction deserves attention even with the missed P value.

The open problem is transfer. The increment was measured against sorafenib, and the change in systemic standard that ended accrual means its size on a newer backbone is unknown. A more active systemic regimen could shrink the benefit by controlling liver disease itself, or enlarge it by holding extrahepatic disease long enough that intrahepatic control decides survival. That question, more than this trial's P value, determines whether liver SBRT becomes routine in first-line advanced HCC.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Personalized 27.5-50 Gy in 5 fractions was deliverable in a cohort with 74.0% macrovascular invasion without more G3+ TRAE (47% vs 42%, P=.52). PFS HR 0.55 is the RT-attributable read; local control and in-liver failure patterns are not reported in source text, and the dose range blocks any dose-response read.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: SBRT followed by sorafenib extended median PFS from 5.5 to 9.2 mo with G3+ TRAE 47% vs 42% (P=.52), so it did not compromise systemic tolerability. The trial closed after the first-line systemic standard changed, leaving the increment over newer backbones untested and the sequencing with systemic therapy an open planning question.

papers.title: Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy vs Sorafenib Alone in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: The NRG Oncology/RTOG 1112 Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Most patients with locally advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recur within the liver following systemic therapy.

OBJECTIVE: To determine whether stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) improves outcomes in patients with locally advanced HCC compared with sorafenib alone.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter phase 3 randomized clinical trial randomized patients with HCC 1:1 to sorafenib or SBRT followed by sorafenib, stratified by performance status, liver function, degree of metastases, and macrovascular invasion. Eligible patients had HCC unsuitable for or refractory to standard local-regional therapies and were candidates for first-line systemic therapy. Data were collected from April 2013 to March 2021, and data were analyzed from July 2022 to August 2023.

INTERVENTION: Personalized SBRT, 27.5 to 50 Gy in 5 fractions.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was overall survival (OS). Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS), adverse events, and quality of life.

RESULTS: Of 193 patients randomized, 177 were eligible. Accrual was stopped early due to a change in standard-of-care systemic therapy. Of 177 included patients, 150 (84.7%) were male, and the median (IQR) age was 66 (60-72) years. Macrovascular invasion was seen in 131 (74.0%). As of July 1, 2022, the median OS was 12.3 months (90% CI, 10.6-14.3) with sorafenib vs 15.8 months (90% CI, 11.4-19.2) following SBRT and sorafenib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.77; 90% CI, 0.59-1.01; 1-sided P = .06). Adjusting for stratification factors, OS was improved with SBRT (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.52-0.99; 2-sided P = .04). Median PFS was improved from 5.5 months (95% CI, 3.4-6.3) with sorafenib to 9.2 months (95% CI, 7.5-11.9) with SBRT and sorafenib (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.40-0.75; 2-sided P < .001). Treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events were seen in 37 of 88 (42%) and 39 of 83 (47%) of patients treated with sorafenib vs SBRT and sorafenib, respectively (P = .52). There were 2 treatment-related deaths in the sorafenib group (death not otherwise specified and liver failure) and 1 in the SBRT and sorafenib group (lung infection). At 6 months, improved quality of life was seen in 2 of 20 (10%) and 6 of 17 (35%) of patients treated with sorafenib and SBRT and sorafenib, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this phase 3 randomized clinical trial, among patients with locally advanced HCC, SBRT was associated with a clinically important but not statistically significant improved overall survival compared with sorafenib alone.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01730937.
